title: North and South: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Milton's Smoke and Margaret's Arrival

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked — a close, passionate, and sometimes heated look at Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel.
I'm your host, and over this series we're going to take the novel apart — its smoke and its tenderness, its fury and its longing.
Today we begin at the beginning: Milton's mills, a displaced family, and a young woman who arrives with all the composure of the South — and slowly has it unmade.
Joining me for the whole series are three people whose thinking I trust completely — and whose disagreements I find absolutely riveting.
First, Dr. Daniel Rosen — a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of power.
Daniel is at his best when he shows you the machinery behind the manners — the class interests hiding inside a polite drawing-room scene.
Second, Prof. James Blackstone — a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant, in practical terms, to be poor, to be accused, or to be tried in Victorian England.
James will keep us honest about the real world the novel is set inside.
And third, Ms. Caroline Woodcourt — a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has, by her own account, never quite left it.
Caroline reads for the music of sentences and the emotional truth of characters — and she will read passages aloud with a relish I find infectious.
Welcome, all three of you.
Now — let's start with arrival.
Margaret Hale comes to Milton as an outsider — the daughter of a dissenting clergyman who has uprooted his family from their genteel southern life.
And almost immediately she is placed in a room with John Thornton.
Caroline — you've read this novel more times than any of us. Where does Gaskell place us, as readers, in those early encounters?
She places us, brilliantly, inside Thornton's gaze — which is the last place Margaret would want us.
There's a tea-table scene in chapter ten that I've re-read more times than I can count — and it never stops being funny and tender and slightly excruciating, all at once.
Thornton is supposed to be listening to Mr. Hale. He is emphatically not listening to Mr. Hale.
He's watching a bracelet slide down Margaret's wrist and slide back up again.
And Gaskell gives us this wonderful parenthetical thought — he could almost have exclaimed, there it goes again.
It seems as if it fascinated him to see her push it up impatiently until it tightened her soft flesh; and then to mark the loosening — the fall.
The loosening. The fall. Gaskell gives it its own sentence. That's where the feeling lives.
And then the best bit — the sugar-tongs moment.

She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of an unwilling slave; but her eye caught the moment when he was ready for another cup; and he almost longed to ask her to do for him what he saw her compelled to do for her father, who took her little finger and thumb in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues.
The proud air of an unwilling slave — and she's handing him tea.
Gaskell has the whole novel in miniature right there — Margaret performing duty through gritted teeth, and Thornton watching her with a longing he can't yet name.
That phrase — unwilling slave — is doing serious work, and I don't think it's accidental.
Margaret has come from a world where grace and service were the currencies of femininity.
And here she is, performing exactly those gestures — for a man she barely tolerates — in a northern industrial town.
Gaskell is showing us that the drawing-room and the factory floor have more in common than either party wants to admit.
There is labour happening in that tea-table scene — social labour, gendered labour — and Margaret is doing it involuntarily.
But what interests me just as much is what happens later in the novel — when the real cost of submission to authority arrives, and it's not metaphorical at all.
Mrs. Hale tells Margaret about Frederick — about the mutiny, about learning through a newspaper that her son's name was not among those rescued.
This is a family destroyed by a system — by the Royal Navy's absolute authority over individual conscience.
And Gaskell renders it in the body — in Mr. Hale's walk home from Southampton.
He came at last, his arms hanging loose down, his head sunk, and walking heavily along, as if every step was a labour and a trouble.
His arms hanging loose. Every step a labour and a trouble.
That is a man broken by an institution. And Gaskell doesn't let us look away.
What Daniel's describing — Frederick branded a traitor by a newspaper before any verdict — is historically precise, not literary licence.
Naval mutiny in this period was one of the gravest offences in English law — carrying the death penalty, and tried by court martial, not by civilian jury.
And the press reported lists of names — officers saved, men condemned — before families had any official word.
So the Hales scanning a newspaper for their son's name — hoping Carr is a misprint for Hale — that is exactly how it would have worked.
The state communicates its verdicts through newspapers before it communicates them to the people most affected.
What strikes me too is the quote from Mrs. Hale about finding her husband — the scene she describes by the Oldham beech-tree.

And when I got to him, he did not speak, or seem surprised to see me there, more than three miles from home, beside the Oldham beech-tree; but he put my arm in his, and kept stroking my hand, as if he wanted to soothe me to be very quiet under some great heavy blow.
That stoicism — stroking her hand, saying nothing — is the behaviour of someone who has already processed the worst, and is now managing someone else's grief.
It's a portrait of a marriage under institutional catastrophe. And it's heartbreaking.
And the novel carries that weight — the family's catastrophe — right into the new world of Milton.
It's why Margaret is who she is. She is not simply a southern girl with airs — she's someone who has already lived through loss.
And the novel earns Thornton's obsession with her because we feel that history in her composure.
There is that extraordinary moment after the riot — when Thornton walks through Milton undone.
Almost sick with longing for that one half-hour — that one brief space of time when she clung to him, and her heart beat against his — to come once again.
That one half-hour. Gaskell measures great feeling in the smallest units of time.
And it rhymes, doesn't it, with the tea-table — with the bracelet, with the sugar-tongs — the same man, reduced to watching, to wanting what he can't ask for.
That passage also contains something else, though — Thornton has just come from the borough court, from dealing with the riot cases.
He has just charged the police to be on the watch — his words, essentially — for the swift right arm of the law.
The swift right arm of the law should be in readiness to strike, as soon as they could prove a fault.
And then he walks out into the street and dissolves into longing for Margaret.
Gaskell is doing something very precise there — she is showing us that the man administering the law is not a cold mechanism.
He is also — simultaneously — a man sick with grief and desire.
Which makes the law more dangerous, not less. Because it's personal.
James, from a legal-historical perspective — is that a fair reading of the magistracy at this period?
Were the men administering industrial justice also the men who owned the mills?
Overwhelmingly, yes.
The Justices of the Peace in industrial towns in this period were drawn almost exclusively from the manufacturing and commercial class.
There was no pretence of separation between economic interest and judicial power.
When Thornton charges the police to watch for fault — he is, quite literally, a mill owner directing state force against his own workers.
Gaskell knew this. She lived in Manchester. She saw it.
And to Daniel's point — the fact that Thornton is also a man in anguish does not dissolve that structural reality.
It complicates it. Which is what great novels do.
That tension — between the personal and the structural, between longing and law — is going to be at the heart of everything we discuss today.
We've seen Margaret arrive — composed, performing, seen but not seeing herself seen.
And we've had a first glimpse of what the novel is willing to cost its characters.
Coming up — we'll move deeper into the mill, the strike, and what Gaskell asks us to feel about both sides of that confrontation.

segments.title: The Weight of Industry: Thornton, Strikes, and Social Order

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the podcast that takes Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the engine room of the novel — the world of mills, money, and the social order that holds it all together.
With me today are three brilliant readers of this novel, each bringing a very different lens.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in a novel as a mechanism of class power — and he's particularly good at finding the radical nerve in a writer who didn't always know she had one.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real-world texture — what the law actually was, what it meant to be poor, what the institutions depicted in fiction actually did.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader of classic fiction who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Today's segment focuses on Thornton — his power, his place in the social order, and the extraordinary moment when Margaret offers him her money and something much harder to name.
Caroline, let's start with the first impression — because Gaskell stages it so carefully.
The first meeting between Margaret and Thornton is one of those passages I return to every time I re-read the novel.
Because Gaskell does something quietly brilliant — she gives us the scene entirely from Thornton's perspective of discomfiture, while Margaret remains perfectly composed.
And then comes this description of how Margaret looks — and Gaskell reaches for something imperial.
"a large Indian shawl, which hung about her in long heavy folds, and which she wore as an empress wears her drapery."
An empress.
Not a lady, not a beauty — an empress.
And yet her dress is plain — a straw bonnet with white ribbon.
Gaskell is telling us that Margaret's authority is entirely in her bearing, her selfhood — and that it immediately wrong-foots a man accustomed to being the dominant figure in every room.
I'd push on that word 'empress' a little, because it's doing double work.
Yes, it signals Margaret's natural authority — but the shawl itself is Indian.
We're in the 1850s.
The empire is the backdrop against which northern manufacturing operates — the cotton that feeds Thornton's mills comes from that empire, literally.
So Margaret walks in draped in imperial cloth and carries it like sovereignty — and Gaskell may not have been fully conscious of the irony, but it's there.
What interests me more, though, is what Margaret says about Thornton the moment she's back with her mother.
She gives a verdict — measured, a little condescending — and the condescension is itself class ideology in miniature.
"Altogether a man who seems made for his niche, mamma; sagacious, and strong, as becomes a great tradesman."
Made for his niche.
She's praised him and boxed him in simultaneously — he belongs in trade, and trade is beneath her.
That phrase — 'great tradesman' — would have landed with particular force for Gaskell's readers.
The Victorian hierarchy of occupations was extraordinarily precise and largely unwritten — but everyone understood it.
A clergyman's daughter — even an impoverished one — outranked a manufacturer almost automatically in the social ledger.
And yet the manufacturer had the money — often far more of it.
That tension — between inherited cultural prestige and new industrial wealth — is precisely what the novel is built on.
And Gaskell dramatises it through Margaret's very syntax — she praises him with the words she'd use for a well-made tool.
That's exactly right — and Gaskell knows it's not the final word.
Because a few chapters later Margaret catches herself and says something much more interesting — about what a lady actually is.
She's defending herself to her mother — who has the full weight of southern gentility behind her — and she says, wonderfully:
"I am myself a born and bred lady through it all, even though it comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes."
That sentence is doing something radical for 1855.
She is uncoupling ladyhood from leisure — saying that gentility is a quality of character, not an exemption from work.
And in that gesture, she is — without knowing it — beginning to meet Thornton on his own terms.
There's a mirror image of that self-defence happening on the Thornton side, and it's just as fierce — perhaps fiercer.
Mrs. Thornton's interior monologue about her son is one of the great outbursts of maternal pride in Victorian fiction.
She's learned that Margaret has condescended to John, and the response is volcanic.
"Boy and man, he's the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don't care if I am his mother; I can see what's what, and not be blind."
That last clause — 'I can see what's what, and not be blind' — is everything.
She's asserting that her judgment is reliable precisely because she loves him — which is the opposite of how we usually discount a mother's testimony.
And Gaskell validates it — because John Thornton is exactly what his mother says he is.
The class antagonism here is genuinely symmetrical, which is unusual in Victorian fiction.
Most novels of the period show deference flowing upward — toward the gentry, toward the cultivated.
What Gaskell gives us is two families, each entirely convinced of its own superiority — and each, the narrative quietly insists, partly right.
It's a structural irony that keeps the novel honest.
And there's an interesting counterpoint to all of this pride and condescension — the moment Margaret befriends the Higgins family.
Because what she finds in Milton, once she has that human connection, is not what she expected.
That passage about Milton becoming brighter is one I find quietly devastating, actually.
Gaskell rules out all the obvious explanations — it's not the better weather, it's not the passage of time softening her.
She pares it back to something very simple.
"It was that in it she had found a human interest."
A human interest.
Not a political awakening, not a conversion to the cause of labour — just the simple transformative fact of knowing and caring about specific people.
Gaskell is making a claim here about how social understanding actually works — it begins with individual recognition, not with ideology.
I won't entirely disagree with Caroline on that — but I'd add a caveat.
The 'human interest' Margaret finds is in the Higgins family — working people, people whose lungs are being destroyed by the mills.
So the emotional education that makes Milton bearable for her is being funded, in a sense, by the suffering she doesn't yet fully see.
Gaskell is a kinder novelist than she perhaps should be — but the darker reading is available, if you want it.
That tension — between sympathy and structural critique — is exactly what the novel never quite resolves, which is part of its greatness.
And it brings us to the scene I most wanted to discuss today — the extraordinary moment in Chapter 52 when Margaret offers Thornton her money.
James, you've written about the legal dimension of this scene — can you set it up for us?
The scene is almost scandalously bold when you put it in its historical context.
A single woman in 1855 had the legal right to own and dispose of property — that was one advantage of not being married.
Once married, under coverture, her assets would pass to her husband.
So Margaret's offer is a function of her independence — and Gaskell makes sure Margaret understands the transaction in those terms.
She frames it with meticulous precision — even down to the interest rate.

"if you would take some money of mine, eighteen hundred and fifty-seven pounds, lying just at this moment unused in the bank, and bringing me in only two and a half per cent.—you could pay me much better interest, and might go on working Marlborough Mills."
Two and a half per cent.
She has done the arithmetic.
She knows what government consols yield, she knows what a manufacturer could offer — and she arrives not as a benefactress but as an investor making a rational case.
And yet the prose tells us her hands are trembling as she searches for the documents.
The words are businesslike — the body is not.
Gaskell writes that Margaret is 'most anxious to have it all looked upon in the light of a mere business arrangement, in which the principal advantage would be on her side.'
'Most anxious' — she is protesting too much, and we can see it, and Thornton can see it, and she cannot quite admit what it means.
What I love most is what happens next — or rather, what Gaskell withholds.
She writes that 'her very heart-pulse was arrested by the tone in which Mr. Thornton spoke' — and then she ends the scene there.
'His voice was hoarse, and trembling with tender passion' — and the words themselves never come.
The chapter ends on silence.
The silence matters economically as well as romantically.
Think about what Margaret's offer actually represents: she is proposing to become a stakeholder in industrial production.
The gentry's capital — inherited, passive — flowing into the northern mill.
This is the structural resolution of the novel's central conflict — north and south, literally pooling resources.
And Gaskell has the nerve to frame it as a financial instrument — loan documents, a stated rate of return — before she lets it become love.
That's not a compromise of the romance — that is the romance, for this novel.
A romance conducted in the language of interest rates — which may be the most accurate description of North and South I've ever heard.
We've moved from that first moment of mutual astonishment in the sitting-room, through all the pride and condescension and counter-pride, to this trembling silence over a bank statement.
And somehow Gaskell has made it feel utterly inevitable.
Coming up, we'll turn to the Higgins household and what the novel actually knows — and doesn't know — about the experience of working people.

segments.title: Class, Cotton, and Conscience: The North's Moral Crisis

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the show that takes Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel seriously — as seriously as she did.
I'm your host, and today we're spending our time in what I'd call the moral engine room of the novel — the zone where class, conscience, and cotton mills grind against each other.
Joining me are three guests who bring very different lenses to this material.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he will not let the comfortable off the hook.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the hard institutional context — what the mill towns actually were, what poverty actually meant.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader who has lived with this novel for years and knows exactly which sentences break your heart and why.
Our segment today is titled Class, Cotton, and Conscience: The North's Moral Crisis.
We're tracking how Gaskell builds relationships across the class divide — and what those relationships cost, and reveal.
Daniel, I'd like to start with you — because the novel's opening moves in Milton are, in a sense, about a Southern woman learning to see the working poor as individuals.
What's Gaskell doing in those early street scenes with Margaret and the workmen?
What Gaskell is doing is structurally significant — and quietly subversive.
Margaret arrives in Milton as an outsider whose aesthetic education has taught her to register landscape and manners — not labour.
And Gaskell forces her — forces us — to encounter the working class not as a mass, but as faces with voices.
There's one man who stands out from the crowd because he speaks to her — not crudely, but with a kind of weary grace.
"You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face."
Now, a lesser novelist uses that as charm — a bit of Northern colour.
Gaskell uses it to establish a silent bond — what she calls, quite precisely, a "silent recognition."
That's not sentimentality — that's the novel insisting that the working poor have an inner life that the class system conspires to make invisible.
And what's remarkable is that Gaskell gives us that recognition before Margaret even knows his name.
She says they have never exchanged a word beyond that first compliment — yet she looks upon him with more interest than upon anyone else in Milton.
That is doing a lot of work in a sentence.
More interesting than the mill owners, more interesting than the men who will later court her.
And then she sees him on Sundays with his daughter — described as, if possible, still more unhealthy than he was himself.
That small parenthetical phrase — "if possible" — carries enormous weight.
It's Gaskell glancing at the reader with controlled horror — this is what the mills do to people over generations.
That detail about the daughter is not accidental — it's historically precise.
Fluff lung — byssinosis — was endemic among cotton workers in the 1840s and 1850s.
Young women who worked the cards and the looms inhaled cotton dust from childhood — many were dead before thirty.
Gaskell had access to this — her husband was a Unitarian minister in Manchester, and they moved in circles that saw the wreckage firsthand.
What she does in the very next passage is tell us about the girl's face lighting up at the sight of hedge flowers from the South.
Dog-violets and lesser celandines — flowers of fields this girl has almost certainly never walked in.
"Her pale blue eyes lightened up as she took them, and her father spoke for her."
He speaks for her because she is too weak or too stunned by simple kindness to speak for herself.
That detail — the father speaking — is devastating in its understatement.
And the father — Higgins — becomes absolutely central to the novel's argument about what solidarity actually looks like.
When Mr. Hale dies, it's Higgins who comes to Margaret — not the respectable middle-class acquaintances of Milton, not Thornton.
And he's been turned away by the servants, which is a perfect miniature of the class system in action.
But listen to how he speaks of Mr. Hale — this is extraordinary.
"There's as good a man gone as ever lived on this earth, let who will be t'other!"
"Let who will be t'other" — that is a man gesturing at the entire social hierarchy and dismissing it in five words.
Mr. Hale was a gentleman who lost his living — who lost everything the class system rewards — and Higgins sees him clearly anyway.
That's moral vision. And it comes from below, not from above.
I find that passage almost unbearably moving — and partly because of the dialect.
Gaskell renders Higgins's speech phonetically — "yo' might ha' knocked me down wi' a straw" — and some readers have found that condescending.
I think they have it backwards.
The dialect is a mark of respect — Gaskell is insisting that this man's actual voice, his actual cadences, belong on the page.
The gentlemen in this novel speak standard English — correct, measured, sometimes bloodless.
Higgins speaks with texture and heat. The language itself is a class argument.
That's a crucial point — and it connects to what Thornton eventually comes to understand, painfully and slowly.
Gaskell gives us an unusually frank anatomy of Thornton's ideology at the moment it begins to crack.
He is, we are told, an architect of his own fortunes — the self-made man who attributes everything to commerce's fair and open road.
He and the workers have "led parallel lives — very close, but never touching."
That is not merely a description of Thornton — it's a description of an entire class's deliberate incuriosity about those beneath them.
And what breaks that pattern is not legislation, not charity — it's a single human encounter with Higgins, outside the master-and-workman frame.
Gaskell is making a pointed argument here about what structural change actually requires at its root.
James is right — and I want to press on that phrase Gaskell gives Thornton through the narrator.
Once the two men are brought face to face — and this is crucial — it happens outside the character of master and workman.
Only then do they each begin to recognise —
"we have all of us one human heart."
Gaskell is borrowing from Wordsworth there — knowingly, I think.
But she gives it an industrial-era precision that Wordsworth's pastoral never quite managed.
The recognition only comes when the economic relationship is temporarily suspended.
Which raises the uncomfortable question: what kind of system requires you to forget your power over someone before you can see them as human?
That question hangs over the whole novel's ending, doesn't it.
Because by the time Thornton faces ruin in chapter fifty-two, his transformation has come too late to save him commercially.
And when Lennox tries to counsel him — Lennox, the man of easy London success — Thornton refuses to hear it.
He says something to Margaret that I think is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the book.
"to find oneself no longer young — yet thrown back to the starting-point which requires the hopeful energy of youth."
"To feel one half of life gone, and nothing done — nothing remaining of wasted opportunity, but the bitter recollection that it has been."
That's not just a man lamenting bankruptcy — that is a man confronting the cost of a life built entirely on the wrong metric.
And Gaskell gives those words to a man who was, by any Victorian standard, a success — until the system that made him ate him.
The cotton trade was genuinely volatile — credit collapses, market contractions, the American South cutting off supply.
Thornton is historically plausible — a man who did everything right by his own code and still went under.
What's devastating is that his line — those who are happy and successful are too apt to make light of the misfortunes of others — could have been Higgins speaking.
It's the kind of thing the working poor have always known.
Thornton only arrives at it when he falls far enough to glimpse the view from below.
That's a remarkable place to pause — the master and the mill worker converging, through suffering, on the same hard truth.
Daniel, James, Caroline — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the question of what women are permitted to know, and to say, in this novel — and what happens when Margaret says too much.

segments.title: Margaret's Wit and the Art of Survival

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've been tracking Margaret Hale across a novel that keeps demanding more of her — more composure, more sacrifice, more wit deployed in rooms that weren't built for her.
This segment we're going deep into Chapter Ten — a single evening visit that is one of the most compressed, most electrically charged scenes Gaskell ever wrote.
Caroline Woodcourt is here as our close reader — she's been re-reading this chapter, she tells me, all week.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads every drawing-room conversation as a map of class power — and Chapter Ten gives him a great deal to work with.
And Prof. James Blackstone brings us the social and institutional reality behind what these characters think they're talking about.
Caroline — you wanted to start with the room itself, with what Margaret sees when she looks up from her sewing.
Yes — because this is such a precise act of observation, and it tells us everything about who Margaret is becoming.
She's been sitting quietly, doing her needlework, listening to her father and Thornton talk.
Then her mother says something trivial, she glances up — and she sees the two men as if for the first time.
Gaskell gives us this extraordinary portrait of Thornton's face.
"The straight brows fell low over the clear, deep-set, earnest eyes, which without being unpleasantly sharp, seemed intent enough to penetrate into the very heart and core of what he was looking at."
That phrase — 'the very heart and core' — that's not neutral description.
Margaret is already being seen by those eyes, even as she watches them.
And what she notices — what she actually admires first — is not his power or his money, but his smile.
That physical description is doing more than romantic groundwork, though.
Look at how Gaskell constructs the contrast between Hale and Thornton — the soft, wavering lines of the clergyman against the face carved in marble.
One man's features register every fluctuation of feeling; the other's are set, resolved, ready — in Gaskell's exact phrase — 'to do and dare everything.'
That is the face of industrial capital, not metaphorically — literally.
Thornton's will has been formed by a system that requires exactly that quality — the suppression of hesitation, of sympathy, in the service of production.
The smile, when it comes, is described as almost childlike — because that's the only moment the system lets him off the hook.
That's a fair reading, Daniel, though I'd note the comparison cuts both ways.
Mr. Hale's softness is also a form of evasion — his fluctuating features are those of a man who has consistently declined to make hard choices.
What's remarkable is that Margaret sees all of this — and yet the tension of the chapter erupts not between the two men, but between Margaret and Thornton.
She is defending the South against his implied condescension, and she doesn't hold back.
That speech of Margaret's is one of my favourite moments in the whole novel.
She's been sitting quietly, and then something in Thornton's tone rouses her — and she speaks with 'fond vehemence,' which is such a Gaskell phrase.
The anger and the love are completely inseparable.
And then she delivers this indictment of what she sees on the streets of Milton.
"I see men here going about in the streets who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care — who are not only sufferers but haters."
'Not only sufferers but haters' — she's twenty years old and she has just described class resentment with more precision than most political theorists manage.
And then she collapses into silence, angry with herself for having said so much.
That sentence should be printed on a wall somewhere.
The full passage is worth holding in view.
"There is not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of injustice which I see here."
A sullen sense of injustice — not poverty alone, not hunger alone, but the awareness that the system is rigged.
Margaret sees what Thornton refuses to see precisely because his position depends on not seeing it.
Her outsider status — her Southernness, her gender, her powerlessness in this world — is exactly what gives her vision its clarity.
Historically, what she's observing is entirely accurate.
The 1840s and 50s in the English industrial towns produced exactly that physiognomy of grievance — it's what alarmed every reformer who walked those streets.
What's remarkable is that Gaskell gives this insight not to a political economist or a trade unionist, but to a vicar's daughter from Hampshire — and she says it directly to the mill-owner's face.
Thornton, of course, has his response — but it comes later, on the stairs, muttered to himself.
Oh, that exit line — I love it so much because it's so transparently wounded.
He has just met a woman who argued him to a standstill, and this is what he produces on the way out.
"A more proud, disagreeable girl I never saw. Even her great beauty is blotted out of one's memory by her scornful ways."
He's trying to dismiss her, and he can't even do it without confessing she's beautiful.
The word 'blotted out' is doing extraordinary work — you only try to blot out something that is very much still present.
Gaskell is being wickedly comic here, and I think she knows exactly what she's doing.
Gaskell always knows what she's doing — which is why that comedy sits so close to something much darker in this chapter.
We move from the sparring in the drawing room to Margaret alone with her anxiety about her mother.
And that passage has a quality of dread that is almost Gothic in its accumulation of small signs.
Dixon comes out of the bedroom crying and cross — her mistress's suffering converted instantly into the servant's irritability.
Margaret goes in and finds something she was never meant to see.
"She caught a few words which were evidently a prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily suffering."
A prayer for endurance, not for recovery — this is a woman who already knows what is coming.
And the cause of that suffering is not abstract — Gaskell is careful to name it.
It's Milton itself: the air 'deprived of all revivifying principle,' the domestic worries pressing 'in so new and sordid a form.'
The industrial town is literally killing Mrs. Hale, and Gaskell renders this without melodrama — just accumulating domestic detail.
Margaret's response is utterly characteristic: she lies awake planning practical remedies — another servant, more help for Dixon.
She cannot fix what is wrong, but she can organize around the edges of it — and that is what survival looks like in this novel.
That's exactly it — and what moves me most is what's withheld between Margaret and her mother.
Margaret yearns to 're-unite the bond of intimate confidence' — that's the phrase Gaskell uses.
She tries with caresses and soft words, she gets them back — and still feels the secret locked away.
We've just watched this young woman argue with a mill-owner about political economy with absolute fearlessness.
And here she is, unable to reach her own mother — shut out by love, not hostility.
That tension — between Margaret's formidable public self and the private grief she can't quite access — is something we'll be tracing through the rest of the novel.
Daniel, Caroline, James — thank you.
After the break, we'll be turning to Thornton on his own ground — and asking what kind of power he actually holds, and over whom.

segments.title: The Language of Change: How Gaskell Shapes Understanding

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've been tracing how Elizabeth Gaskell builds her world sentence by sentence — and today we're sitting with some of the novel's most charged moments.
Moments where language doesn't just describe feeling — it enacts it.
With me today are three guests who bring very different lenses to this novel.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose work asks what institutions actually do to people — and he reads Gaskell with a forensic eye for exactly that.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and he finds Gaskell more radical than she perhaps intended.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and brings us back to the experience of reading — the sentences that make you stop, re-read, and breathe.
James, I want to start with you — because you're working with passages that span the very intimate and the very public, from Thornton alone with his thoughts to Higgins in the factory yard.
What does Gaskell's language actually do when it shifts between those registers?
What strikes me most is that Gaskell doesn't soften the transitions between registers — she makes you feel the jolt.
Take the passage where Thornton is left alone after the riot.
He's supposed to be attending to the business of the police-office — a matter of public order, of law, of the mill master's civic duty.
And instead, Gaskell gives us this.
"Everything seemed dim and vague beyond—behind—besides the touch of her arms round his neck—the soft clinging which made the dark colour come and go in his cheek as he thought of it."
That syntax is doing something very precise.
The em dashes — "beyond — behind — besides" — enact the mind's failure to locate itself in any stable direction.
A man of iron discipline, and his own grammar is breaking down around a physical memory.
That's exactly it — the dashes are the thought stuttering.
And then Gaskell lands on the body — "the dark colour come and go in his cheek."
This is a man blushing at his own recollection.
Gaskell is so good at that — at catching the body betraying the mind before the mind has caught up.
And immediately adjacent to that private dissolution is Mrs. Thornton.
In the very next passage I'm looking at, she performs her role with absolute external composure — she kisses her son, she speaks coldly, she exits slowly and majestically.
And then Gaskell delivers this with almost brutal economy.
"But when she got into her own, she locked the door, and sate down to cry unwonted tears."
"Unwonted" — that single word carries the weight of a whole characterisation.
These are tears she does not know how to weep, from a woman who has never permitted herself the luxury of self-pity.
I want to hold onto that word — "unwonted" — because it tells us something about Gaskell's whole project in these interior passages.
She consistently reserves the most precise psychological language for the moments when the social performance fails.
Mrs. Thornton's public self is all sharp command and cold authority — the servants notice her directions are suddenly confused, uncertain, because the armour has cracked.
But what Gaskell is very shrewd about is that she doesn't sentimentalise these cracks.
The tears are locked behind a door.
And then there's Margaret's collapse, which I think is one of the most startling passages in the novel.
Gaskell builds it with these tiny, halting verbs — paused, tottered, paused, swayed, fell.
Each one feels like a step toward something inevitable.
"Then she went into the study, paused—tottered forward—paused again—swayed for an instant where she stood, and fell prone on the floor in a dead swoon."
That rhythm — the repetition of "paused" — is almost like watching a body negotiate with gravity.
She holds herself up as long as conscience and will can manage, and then they can't.
The body here is enacting what the social code has forbidden Margaret to say aloud.
She has just committed perjury to protect her brother — or as close to it as a young Victorian woman could come.
And there's no institution — no law, no church, no family — she can turn to for absolution.
The collapse is the only honest response available to her.
Which is why the contrast with Higgins is so structurally important.
Where Margaret collapses under the weight of an impossible private lie, Higgins speaks with absolute public clarity about a structural one.
The employers are demanding loyalty oaths — pledges that workers will not support the Union, will not help those who are striking and starving.
And Higgins names it precisely.

"There's not the pressure on all the broad earth that would make me. Hampers—that's where I worked—makes their men pledge 'emselves they'll not give a penny to help th' Union or keep turn-outs fro' clemming."
"Clemming" — starving — is the word the masters never say in this novel.
Higgins says it plainly, in dialect, in public, and dares the novel's reader to look away.
What I love about that speech is that Gaskell gives him the full argument — not just the defiant refusal, but the moral reasoning.
He says the pledges don't stop men from giving — they just make men into liars.
The employer has already decided what a working man's conscience is worth.
And Higgins refuses that valuation absolutely.
He ends that speech with the consequence: "I dunnot see where I'm to get a shilling."
That is Gaskell at her most politically honest.
Moral integrity in this system doesn't come with a reward — it comes with destitution.
And that is historically precise.
These anti-union pledges were real — they were a standard instrument of industrial coercion throughout the 1840s and 1850s.
To refuse one was, in practical terms, to refuse employment.
What Gaskell does — and this is where her sociology is sharp — is show that the pledge is not just economic coercion.
It reaches into the man's very sense of what he owes his neighbour.
What's remarkable is that all of these passages — the blushing millmaster, the weeping mother, the collapsing Margaret, the defiant Higgins — are written by the same hand, in the same novel.
Gaskell's range is extraordinary — and what we've been hearing today is how her language at every level, from a stutter of dashes to a single dialect word, does the intellectual and emotional work.
We'll be back very shortly with more — stay with us.

segments.title: Crossing Lines: Thornton's Recognition and Margaret's Choice

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the programme where we slow down and sit with one of the great Victorian novels — Elizabeth Gaskell's North and South.
Today we are deep inside the novel's human crossings — the moments where class, faith, labour, and longing press against each other in ways that still feel urgent.
With me today are three people who bring very different eyes to Gaskell's world.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who insists that Gaskell was more radical than she herself knew.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the hard institutional reality behind the novel's world — what poverty actually meant, what the law actually permitted.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has loved this novel since she was a teenager and who pays close, devoted attention to what Gaskell's sentences actually do on the page.
Let's begin with Nicholas Higgins — a man who announces his creed with the bluntness of a hammer on stone.
What strikes me first about Higgins is that Gaskell gives him not a complaint but a epistemology.
He doesn't simply say he's suffering — he tells you how he knows what he knows.
And his speech to Margaret is a direct rebuke to abstract faith — to any belief that floats free of material evidence.
Listen to how he puts it — and this is Gaskell giving him the best lines in the room:
"I believe what I see, and no more. That's what I believe, young woman. I don't believe all I hear—no! not by a big deal."
That "no! not by a big deal" — the exclamation mark, the vernacular idiom — that is a man who has learned his philosophy the hard way.
And yet immediately after the creed, tenderness.
He describes watching Bessy flush with excitement at the sound of a strange step — watching her without her knowing he was watching.
And that juxtaposition is everything, isn't it.
Higgins lands this hard, materialist credo — and then the very next breath is an act of exquisite, private observation.
He noticed. He kept quiet about it. He let Bessy have her hope.
That's not the behaviour of a man who only believes what he sees — that's the behaviour of a man who loves carefully.
And it deepens Bessy too — this woman who is dying, whose body is being consumed by the fluff of the mills, and whose spirit reaches for something beyond the material.
Gaskell gives her a verse from Revelation — and it is devastating in its simplicity:
"They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more: neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat."
She murmurs it after a feverish draught of water — and the physical and the spiritual collapse into each other completely.
It's worth pausing on what that fever and that thirst actually meant in a mill town in the 1850s.
Bessy's condition — the lung disease caused by cotton fluff — was not incidental suffering.
It was the predictable, documented, entirely preventable product of unregulated mill conditions.
Factory commissioners were writing about it. Mill owners knew.
So when Bessy reaches for a verse about the end of heat and thirst, Gaskell's readers in 1855 would have felt the irony with considerable force.
Bessy is dying of heat — of actual, industrial heat — and her consolation is a promise of its absence.
And Gaskell doesn't let Higgins's materialism off the hook either — even as she honours it.
Because the tension in this chapter is precisely between two ways of responding to suffering: faith and collective action.
Higgins believes in solidarity, in the union, in material organisation.
But by chapter thirty-seven, when the strike has failed and the men are broken, Margaret has to talk him out of a very different plan — emigration south.
And her speech against it is one of the most remarkable passages in the novel.
She is not romanticising the South — she is anatomising it with the same relentless precision Higgins uses about the mills:

"Those that have lived there all their lives, are used to soaking in the stagnant waters. They labour on from day to day, in the great solitude of steaming fields—never speaking or lifting up their poor, bent, downcast heads."
"Stagnant waters." "Steaming fields." She is using pastoral vocabulary to describe pastoral hell.
This is Margaret Hale, daughter of a Hampshire vicar, dismantling the mythology of rural England with a fury that is all the more devastating for being completely unsentimental.
I have to come back to that speech — because what strikes me is how completely it shows Margaret's transformation.
In the early chapters, she is the girl who looks down on Milton — who finds the North harsh and graceless and hard.
And she is not entirely wrong about Thornton's boastfulness, let's be clear.
But even in that early moment of criticism, Gaskell shows us Margaret capable of discernment:

"Everything else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so simply—with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother."
She finds the one thing that is genuine in him — and she names it.
His having been a shop-boy is what she likes best of all.
Not the industrialist, not the magistrate — the boy who worked his way up with his mother watching.
What that passage also tells us is something important about class anxiety in the period.
Margaret's charge — that Thornton shows no duty to improve his workers — is not merely a personal grievance.
It maps precisely onto the paternalist critique of Manchester School economics that was very much alive in the 1850s.
Carlyle had been making it. Disraeli had fictionalised it. Gaskell was joining a real public argument.
And the irony Gaskell deploys is sharp — Margaret, the gentry girl, is more alive to the social obligations of industrial wealth than the man who actually holds it.
At least at the start.
That evolution in Thornton is important — but I want to push on what doesn't evolve.
Because by chapter forty-six, we have Margaret in a quite different kind of distress — not about labour, not about class conditions, but about how she stands in Thornton's estimation.
She has compromised herself in his eyes — he saw her at the train station, with a man, and she denied it.
And Gaskell is precise about what Margaret fears losing — not his love, which she has firmly put out of mind, but his regard.
There's a beautiful, wrenching line — Gaskell reaches for a Gerald Griffin poem to express what Margaret cannot say plainly:

"but in the respect and high regard which she had hoped would have ever made him willing, in the spirit of Gerald Griffin's beautiful lines, 'To turn and look back when thou hearest / The sound of my name.'"
She wants, simply, to be the kind of person whose name makes him turn around.
After everything — the strike, the riot, the lie at the station — that is what she is left hoping for.
That is one of the most quietly aching sentences in the novel.
She has held herself so rigidly together — "she kept rigidly to her resolution," Gaskell says — and then this.
The wish is so modest that it breaks your heart.
Not love — just the sound of her name in his mind, making him turn.
And the poem Gaskell reaches for — the poem Margaret imagines — is not her own poem, it's Griffin's.
Margaret is borrowing someone else's words for a feeling she cannot quite claim as her own.
And this is where Gaskell's novel is doing something more nuanced than the standard Victorian marriage plot.
The standard resolution is: misunderstanding cleared, feelings declared, all ends well.
But Gaskell is tracking something reputational — something institutional, almost — about how women's moral credibility was constituted in this society.
Being seen unchaperoned with a man was not just socially awkward — it was a matter of legal and social standing.
Margaret's anxiety about Thornton's opinion is not vanity — it is a rational response to a system in which a woman's worth was perpetually on trial.
Perpetually on trial — and yet we've watched her, in the same novel, face down a crowd of striking workers and hold her ground.
The tension between Margaret's public courage and her private vulnerability around Thornton's regard is one of the things that makes this novel feel so alive.
Next, we turn to the question of what Thornton is actually learning — and whether Gaskell lets him learn it fast enough.

segments.title: Closing: The North Transformed, the Self Remade

utterances.text: We've arrived at the final segment of today's episode, and it feels right to end where the novel itself is most quietly devastating.
Margaret Hale is being remade by Milton — by its noise, its poverty, its proud industrial logic.
And yet she carries Helstone inside her like a wound that won't quite close.
We're going to sit with three passages today that capture that tension — the pastoral South, the industrial North, and a single devastating moment of class recognition.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because you've always said the Helstone passages are where Gaskell's prose becomes something close to poetry.
They really are.
What's remarkable is that Margaret has barely spoken of Helstone since she left it.
Gaskell tells us she sees it in dreams — more vivid than life.
And then she opens up to Bessy Higgins — this girl she's just met in the most impoverished circumstances — and out comes everything she's been holding.
The description she gives is extraordinary — listen to this.
"There are great trees standing all about it, with their branches stretching long and level, and making a deep shade of rest even at noonday."
That phrase — a deep shade of rest — isn't just landscape painting.
It's everything Milton is not — it's respite, it's stillness, it's the opposite of the mills.
And the comparison at the end — billowy ferns, just like the sea — it's Margaret reaching for an image large enough to hold what she's lost.
What strikes me about that scene is the social asymmetry that frames it.
Margaret is pouring out this lyrical elegy for her pastoral home — to a girl who is already dying from the cotton fluff in her lungs.
Gaskell doesn't let Margaret or the reader off the hook for that contrast.
The very next passage is just three sentences long, and it's one of the most quietly annihilating things in the novel.
"And I too am nineteen."
Then Gaskell tells us Margaret thought more sorrowfully than Bessy did of the contrast between them.
More sorrowfully than Bessy — that inversion is devastating.
Bessy is the one whose life is being shortened by industrial labour, and yet it is Margaret who feels the heavier grief.
Whether that's Gaskell's irony or Margaret's moral limitation — or both — the reader has to decide.
James is right that Gaskell makes the class disparity structurally visible — but I want to push on what that visibility costs.
Margaret feels sorrow — genuine sorrow — but she cannot speak for a moment because she is trying to keep the emotion down.
Emotion as something to be managed, controlled — that's a bourgeois habitus in its purest form.
Now set that beside Mrs. Thornton, who operates on entirely different social logic.
Mrs. Thornton doesn't offer sorrow — she offers access.
Here is how she puts it — and it's worth hearing the full condescension packed into this offer.

"If Miss Hale changes her mind and condescends to be curious as to the manufactures of Milton, I can only say I shall be glad to procure her admission to print-works, or reed-making, or the more simple operations of spinning carried on in my son's mill."
She uses the word condescends about Margaret — but the condescension is entirely Mrs. Thornton's own.
The mill is power, and Mrs. Thornton wields access to it the way an aristocrat wields a title.
What I love about that Mrs. Thornton passage is that Gaskell is simultaneously skewering her and respecting her.
The phrase every improvement of machinery is to be seen there in its highest perfection — that is genuine civic pride, not mere snobbery.
Mrs. Thornton believes in Milton the way Margaret believes in Helstone.
The difference is that Margaret's love is elegiac and Mrs. Thornton's is combative.
And that says something profound about what it means to belong to a place — whether you mourn it or fight for it.
Caroline's point about belonging is exactly right, and I think it's where the novel does its most original work.
Gaskell is writing at a moment when the idea of place was being violently disrupted by industrialisation — and she refuses the comfortable pastoral response.
Margaret's description of the ferns and the hidden brook — just like the sea — is beautiful, but it's also a memory, not a refuge.
She can't go back.
And Bessy Higgins has never had a pastoral to go back to.
That asymmetry is the engine of the whole novel.
Gaskell puts Margaret and Bessy at the same age — nineteen — precisely to make the structural violence legible.
One girl has trees and velvet turf in her memory.
The other has cotton dust in her lungs and will be dead within the year.
Gaskell was more radical than her own resolution allows — and passages like these are the evidence.
And on that note — the evidence of a novelist who saw more than she could perhaps fully say — we'll bring this episode to a close.
What today's passages have shown us is a Margaret in transition — grieving the South, confronting the North, and measuring herself against lives utterly unlike her own.
My thanks to Caroline Woodcourt, James Blackstone, and Daniel Rosen for a conversation that has, I think, done full justice to Gaskell's extraordinary ambition.
Until next time — keep reading, keep arguing, and don't let anyone tell you the industrial novel is a minor form.

It appeared to Mr. Thornton that all these graceful cares were habitual
to the family; and especially of a piece with Margaret. She stood by the
tea-table in a light-coloured muslin gown, which had a good deal of pink
about it. She looked as if she was not attending to the conversation,
but solely busy with the tea-cups, among which her round ivory hands
moved with pretty, noiseless, daintiness. She had a bracelet on one
taper arm, which would fall down over her round wrist. Mr. Thornton
watched the replacing of this troublesome ornament with far more
attention than he listened to her father. It seemed as if it fascinated
him to see her push it up impatiently until it tightened her soft flesh;
and then to mark the loosening—the fall. He could almost have
exclaimed—“There it goes again!” There was so little left to be done
after he arrived at the preparation for tea, that he was almost sorry
the obligation of eating and drinking came so soon to prevent him
watching Margaret. She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of
an unwilling slave; but her eye caught the moment when he was ready for
another cup; and he almost longed to ask her to do for him what he saw
her compelled to do for her father, who took her little finger and thumb
in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues. Mr.
Thornton saw her beautiful eyes lifted to her father, full of light,
half-laughter, and half-love, as this bit of pantomime went on between
the two, unobserved as they fancied, by any. Margaret’s head still
ached, as the paleness of her complexion, and her silence might have
testified; but she was resolved to throw herself into the breach, if
there was any long untoward pause, rather than that her father’s friend,
pupil, and guest should have cause to think himself in any way
neglected. But the conversation went on; and Margaret drew into a
corner, near her mother, with her work, after the tea-things were taken
away; and felt that she might let her thoughts roam, without fear of
being suddenly wanted to fill up a gap.

the mutiny. Poor Fred! I dare say it was a comfort to him to write it,

be some mistake; for poor Fred was such a fine fellow, only perhaps
rather too passionate; and we hoped that the name of Carr, which was in
the list, was a misprint for that of Hale—newspapers are so careless.
And towards post-time the next day, papa set off to walk to Southampton
to get the papers; and I could not stop at home, so I went to meet him.
He was very late—much later than I thought he would have been; and I
sat down under the hedge to wait for him. He came at last, his arms
hanging loose down, his head sunk, and walking heavily along, as if
every step was a labour and a trouble. Margaret, I see him now.”

The evidence against Boucher, and other ring-leaders of the riot, was
taken before him: that against the three others, for conspiracy, failed.
But he sternly charged the police to be on the watch; for the swift
right arm of the law should be in readiness to strike, as soon as they

bring back the scene,—not of his repulse and rejection the day before,
but the looks, the actions of the day before that. He went along the
crowded streets mechanically, winding in and out among the people, but

half-hour—that one brief space of time when she clung to him, and her
heart beat against his—to come once again.

Margaret opened the door and went in with the straight, fearless,
dignified presence habitual to her. She felt no awkwardness; she had too
much the habits of society for that. Here was a person come on business
to her father; and, as he was one who had shown himself obliging, she
was disposed to treat him with a full measure of civility. Mr. Thornton
was a good deal more surprised and discomfited than she. Instead of a
quiet, middle-aged clergyman, a young lady came forward with frank
dignity,—a young lady of a different type to most of those he was in
the habit of seeing. Her dress was very plain: a close straw bonnet of
the best material and shape, trimmed with white ribbon; a large Indian
shawl, which hung about her in long heavy folds, and which she wore as
an empress wears her drapery. He did not understand who she was, as he
caught the simple, straight, unabashed look, which showed that his
being there was of no concern to the beautiful countenance, and called
up no flush of surprise to the pale ivory of the complexion. He had
heard that Mr. Hale had a daughter, but he had imagined that she was a
little girl.

“Oh, mamma!” said Margaret, lifting herself up, “don’t punish me for so
careless a speech. I don’t mind ironing, or any kind of work for you and
papa. I am myself a born and bred lady through it all, even though it
comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes. I am tired now, just for a

again. And as to Mr. Thornton’s being in trade, why he can’t help that

redeeming—your more than redeeming what you have lost—don’t speak till

rapidly turning over some law papers, and statement of accounts in a
trembling hurried manner. “Oh! here it is! and—he drew me out a
proposal—I wish he was here to explain it—showing that if you would
take some money of mine, eighteen hundred and fifty-seven pounds, lying

working Marlborough Mills.” Her voice had cleared itself and become more

most anxious to have it all looked upon in the light of a mere business

the day look brighter.” And another day, as she was unconsciously
smiling at some passing thought, she was addressed by a poorly-dressed,
middle-aged workman, with, “You may well smile, my lass; many a one
would smile to have such a bonny face.” This man looked so careworn that
Margaret could not help giving him an answering smile, glad to think
that her looks, such as they were, should have had the power to call up
a pleasant thought. He seemed to understand her acknowledging glance,
and a silent recognition was established between them whenever the
chances of the day brought them across each other’s paths. They had
never exchanged a word; nothing had been said but that first compliment;
yet somehow Margaret looked upon this man with more interest than upon
any one else in Milton. Once or twice, on Sundays, she saw him walking
with a girl, evidently his daughter, and, if possible, still more
unhealthy than he was himself.
c8:p20.summary: Margaret encounters a careworn workman who compliments her; later sees him with what appears to be his ailing daughter; a silent recognition and interest develop between them.
c8:p20.best_quote: You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face

c8:p21.text:
One day Margaret and her father had been as far as the fields that lay
around the town; it was early spring, and she had gathered some of the
hedge and ditch flowers, dog-violets, lesser celandines, and the like,
with an unspoken lament in her heart for the sweet profusion of the
South. Her father had left her to go into Milton upon some business; and
on the road home she met her humble friends. The girl looked wistfully
at the flowers, and, acting on a sudden impulse, Margaret offered them
to her. Her pale blue eyes lightened up as she took them, and her father
spoke for her.
c8:p21.summary: Margaret gathers spring flowers and spontaneously offers them to the ailing girl, who receives them gratefully.

c43:p48.text:
“Eh!” said he, as she came in, “to think of th’ oud gentleman dropping
off as he did! Yo’ might ha’ knocked me down wi’ a straw when they
telled me. ‘Mr. Hale?’ said I; ‘him as was th’ parson?’ ‘Ay,’ said they.
‘Then,’ said I, ‘there’s as good a man gone as ever lived on this earth,
let who will be t’other!’ And I came to see yo’, and tell yo’ how
grieved I were, but them women in th’ kitchen wouldn’t tell yo’ I were
there. They said yo’ were ill,—and butter me, but yo’ dunnot look like
the same wench. And yo’re going to be a grand lady up i’ Lunnon, aren’t
yo’?”
c43:p48.summary: Nicholas expresses his grief at Mr. Hale's death, reveals he attempted to visit Margaret earlier but was turned away, notes her changed appearance, and recounts that John Thornton told him Margaret is leaving and will not return.
